working_title: Electric vs Push Golf Trolley: How to Actually Choose for UK Courses
angle: A practical, opinionated guide to deciding between a push and electric trolley aimed at the regular UK walking golfer, structured around real decision factors (course terrain, boot space, playing frequency, budget tier) rather than a generic spec comparison. The post resists declaring one type universally better and instead helps the reader identify which fits their actual situation.
research_notes:
- Push trolleys are lighter and simpler than electric models, fold more compactly, and typically offer more storage on the handle console as standard (sources: Today's Golfer, Golf Monthly)
- Electric trolleys are heavier due to battery and motor hardware, but the user barely notices that weight during a round because they are not pushing it themselves
- Three-wheel push design is generally preferable to two-wheel pull models: pushing weight ahead is easier on the body than twisting one arm behind (source: golfthing.co.uk)
- Old-style two-wheel pull trolleys put additional strain on one side of the body — worth flagging briefly
- Push trolleys suit flatter courses and golfers on tighter budgets; electric trolleys particularly justify their cost on hilly or undulating terrain (sources: Golf Monthly, trolleyguru.co.uk)
- Electric trolleys need charging between rounds — a practical consideration for golfers who store their trolley at a club vs at home
- Battery types: lithium (now standard in mid-to-top range) vs older lead-acid; lithium is lighter, faster-charging, more reliable
- Battery capacity tiers commonly available: 18-hole, 27-hole, 36-hole — match to your typical playing pattern and course undulation
- Electric trolley walk-behind (standard) price range roughly £349–£1,349 in 2026; remote/follow models roughly £799–£1,499 (source: thegolfshoponline.co.uk)
- Push trolley price range: roughly £149–£219 for well-regarded models such as PowaKaddy Micra (~£189, 7.5 kg) and Clicgear 4.0 (~£219, aircraft-grade aluminium) (source: thegolfshoponline.co.uk — prices as of their publication date, flag as approximate)
- Key UK brands in electric: PowaKaddy (founded 1983, based in Sittingbourne, Kent; FX and CT ranges), Motocaddy (SE, M5 GPS, M7 GPS Remote), Stewart Golf (UK-built, premium/remote end)
- Key push trolley brands for UK market: PowaKaddy Micra, Clicgear 4.0, Motocaddy Cube, BagBoy Nitron, Stewart R1-S, Big Max
- Remote/follow electric trolleys: highest convenience (hands-free), heaviest (12–17 kg), highest cost — genuinely niche; most golfers do not need them
- Compact fold matters more for electric trolleys because the battery makes them heavier to lift in and out of the boot
- Boot space is a genuine UK-specific consideration: compact electric models (e.g. PowaKaddy CT range) exist specifically for smaller car boots
- Bag compatibility worth noting: some trolleys work best with proprietary bag systems (e.g. Motocaddy EASILOCK, PowaKaddy MAG-LOK) — not essential but worth awareness
- For golfers who play regularly on undulating UK parkland or links, electric offers meaningful energy conservation over 18 holes; for occasional golfers on flat courses, a push trolley is a sensible, lower-cost choice
- Topic not covered in existing posts: stand bag post exists (what-to-actually-look-for-in-a-golf-stand-bag-for-uk-walking-golfers) but no trolley-specific post published
must_avoid:

- Do not invent specs (weights, battery range figures) not supported by research notes
- No invented quotes from reviewers, pros, or brand representatives
- No medical or injury advice beyond the generic ergonomic point about push-vs-pull strain on the body
- No affiliate links to any trolley brand or retailer unless confirmed in approved-partners.md; mention brands informationally only if not approved
- No financial advice on whether a golfer can or should afford an upgrade; describe cost tiers factually only
